answer.exemplar: The four readings can be added as 12 plus 7 plus 9 plus 5. The associative property allows the student to group them as 12 plus 7 first, giving 19, and then 9 plus 5, giving 14, and finally 19 plus 14, which is 33. questions.learningObjective: explain why a sum is unchanged by reordering its addends
questions.stem: A table of delivery runs lists 95, 62 and 38 loads over three days. A supervisor asks why the total load is the same whatever order the days are added. Explain.

answer.exemplar: The three loads are 95, 62 and 38, and their sum is 195. The commutative property of addition says that swapping two addends does not change the total, so 62 plus 95 plus 38 gives 195 as well, and so does every other order. This is what lets a spreadsheet add a column of days in any sequence and still report the same weekly total. The trap is to expect the order of the days to matter because they happened in a particular sequence, but the sum of addends is independent of that sequence.

questions.explanation: Adding the loads in any order gives 195, because the commutative property says the order of addends never changes a sum. The days happen in sequence, but the total does not depend on it.
questions.hint: Add the three loads in two different orders.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain how an additive inverse cancels an entry
questions.stem: A table of account balances shows one row of negative 62 and another row of plus 62. A clerk asks why the two rows cancel. Explain.

answer.exemplar: A number and its additive inverse always sum to the additive identity, zero. The row of negative 62 and the row of plus 62 are such a pair, because 62 is the opposite of negative 62, so together they add to zero and leave the rest of the table untouched. This is why a credit of 62 dollars exactly repairs a charge of 62 dollars, and why the order of the two rows makes no difference to the total. The trap is to treat the two rows as leaving a remainder of 124, which would mean the opposite of cancelling, since a plus and a minus of the same size always cancel.

questions.explanation: Negative 62 and plus 62 are additive inverses, and a number plus its inverse is zero, so the two rows cancel exactly. The trap is to treat opposite signs as adding.
questions.hint: Add the two rows and see what total they give.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain the role of the additive identity in a running total
questions.stem: A table of ticket adjustments shows a row of 0 between a sale of 42 and a refund of 42. A clerk asks why the 0 row can be ignored. Explain.

answer.exemplar: Zero is the additive identity, so adding it to any running total leaves that total exactly as it was. In the table the 0 row sits between a sale of 42 and a refund of 42, and dropping the 0 row leaves the sale and the refund to cancel, giving a net change of zero. This is what lets a spreadsheet carry a balance down a column without checking the zero rows at all, since they contribute nothing either way. The trap is to treat the 0 row as a separate transaction that must be recorded, when it cannot change any balance at all.

questions.explanation: Zero is the additive identity, so it leaves a running total exactly as it was, and the 0 row can be ignored without changing the balance. The trap is to treat it as a transaction to count.
questions.hint: Add the 0 to any balance and watch what happens.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why a factor of 1 leaves a product unchanged
questions.stem: A table of measurements records each item's weight multiplied by 1 to give a standard reading. A technician asks why the table adds nothing extra. Explain.

answer.exemplar: One is the multiplicative identity, so multiplying any measurement by 1 returns that same measurement. A table of readings such as 23 kg, 41 kg and 17 kg therefore shows 23 kg, 41 kg and 17 kg again after the multiplication by 1, and the column of results is identical to the column of inputs. That is why the standard column is a safe check on the data: it can reveal a reading that was copied incorrectly without adding any new information of its own. The trap is to expect the multiplication to change the values, since only a factor of 0 or a factor of negative 1 would do that.

questions.explanation: One is the multiplicative identity, so multiplying a reading by 1 returns the same reading and the results column matches the inputs column. Only 0 or negative 1 would change the values.
questions.hint: Multiply one reading by 1 and compare it with the original.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why a factor must scale every term in a bracket
questions.stem: A table of club orders shows 6 clubs, each with 3 boxes at 4 dollars plus a 1 dollar handle fee per box. Explain why the total is 78 dollars rather than 73.

answer.exemplar: The table gives each club 3 boxes at 4 dollars, which is 12 dollars of boxes, plus a 1 dollar handle fee on each box, so each club spends 13 dollars and 6 clubs spend 78 dollars. The distributive property shows this as 6 times 3 times 4 plus 6 times 1, which is 72 plus 6. The 73 dollar figure comes from adding the handle fee only once, as if a single box carried the fee for all 6 clubs, but the table says the fee applies to every box of every club.

questions.explanation: The handle fee applies to every box, so 6 times 3 times 4 plus 6 times 1 gives 72 plus 6, which is 78. Counting the fee once would give 73.
questions.hint: Expand the bracket and multiply the 6 by each term.
